opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For me, the most problematic area is predictive AI, specifically systems that claim to predict people's futures and are then used to make consequential decisions about them.

People tend to lump everything under "AI." But generative AI, the chatbots and image generators, is a real technology that has made real progress, even if it's overhyped in places. Predictive AI is different. Tools that claim to predict which job applicant will perform well, which defendant will commit another crime if released on bail, or which patient or student is "at risk" are sold with the same aura of sophistication. When you look at the evidence, they often barely outperform simple baselines, sometimes not much better than a coin flip with a few demographic variables.

There are a few reasons this worries me most. First, the stakes are very high. These systems decide whether someone gets a job, gets released, or gets access to care or benefits. Second, the people affected usually have no idea an algorithm was involved and no meaningful way to contest the decision. Third, there's a fundamental limit here that better engineering won't fix. Predicting individual life outcomes is hard because the future depends on things that haven't happened yet. We've seen this in large-scale studies where researchers had rich data and many teams, and the predictions were still not much better than simple models.

The hype does real damage because it gives institutions cover. A hiring manager or a court can say, "The AI said so," and responsibility diffuses. Vendors make bold accuracy claims that are rarely validated independently, and buyers often lack the expertise to push back. So you end up with snake oil, products that don't and can't work as advertised, being deployed in some of the most important decisions in people's lives.

If I had one message, it would be to ask, for any AI product, what exactly it does and what the evidence is. Generative tools, content moderation, and predictive systems each deserve very different levels of trust. Predictive AI about human behavior is where I'd apply the most skepticism.

r001.rationale: The response says predictive AI systems are sold with an aura of sophistication and often perform only slightly better than simple baselines. It does not identify the marketed systems as basic regression models, so it misses that specific core contribution.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say the most problematic use is in what Sayash Kapoor and I call predictive AI, where you have tools being sold to decide who gets a loan, who gets hired, who gets bail, which patients get extra care, and the claim is that the model can forecast how an individual's life is going to turn out. And that's where the hype does the most damage, because the stakes are so high and the evidence is so thin.

What happens is that a vendor goes to a hospital, or a school district, or a criminal justice agency, and says, we have this AI that can predict who will reoffend or who will drop out, and the decision-makers don't have the expertise to evaluate that claim. Often the accuracy numbers come from the vendor itself, evaluated on data that doesn't look like the real population, and when independent researchers get to test these tools, they frequently find they're barely better than a coin flip, or no better than a simple rule with two or three variables. We saw this with COMPAS, we saw it with the Epic sepsis model, we see it over and over.

And I want to be careful here, because it's not that machine learning doesn't work. In domains like image recognition or language, it genuinely does, and that's exactly what makes predictive AI so seductive. People see the real progress in generative AI and assume the same thing must be true of predicting human behavior. But those are completely different problems. Predicting the future of a person's life is hard for fundamental reasons that more data and bigger models don't fix, because the social world is messy and the people being predicted respond to the predictions.

So the harm isn't just that the tools are inaccurate. It's that they're being used to deny people opportunities, often with no recourse and no way to even know that an algorithm was involved. And the hype is what makes that possible, because it short-circuits the skepticism we'd normally bring to a life-altering decision. If I had to pick one thing, that's it. The hype around generative AI is annoying and sometimes misleading, but the hype around predictive AI is actively hurting people right now.

r001.rationale: The response identifies hype around predictive AI as the most harmful use, but does not say that basic regression models are marketed as far more sophisticated than they are.

astra-6.text:
I think one of the most problematic uses of AI hype is to sell systems that claim to predict people's future behavior, and then use those predictions to make consequential decisions about their lives—who gets hired, who gets a loan, or who gets released before trial.

The hype takes real progress in one area of AI and uses it to lend credibility to a very different application. A system's ability to recognize images or generate fluent text doesn't establish that it can predict whether someone will be a good employee. Those claims need their own evidence.

And the people affected often have very little ability to challenge the result. So this isn't just a question of a company wasting money on a product that doesn't work. Someone can lose an opportunity because a prediction has been given an authority it hasn't earned.

r001.rationale: The response criticizes hype around behavioral prediction systems and consequential decisions, but it does not identify basic regression models being marketed as more sophisticated than they are.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the most problematic use is when hype gives institutions an excuse to avoid accountability. Someone says, “Our AI can predict who will be a good employee, who will commit a crime, or which child is at risk,” and that claim starts to substitute for evidence. These are decisions that can profoundly affect people’s lives.

The issue isn’t just that the system might make mistakes. It’s that we may not have good reason to believe the thing being promised is predictable in the first place. But calling it AI makes it sound scientifically established. And when someone challenges a decision, the institution can point to the technology instead of explaining and defending its own choices.

So the hype I worry about most is the kind that turns speculative claims into authority, especially over people who have very little ability to push back.

r001.rationale: The response criticizes hype that turns speculative AI predictions into authority, but does not identify marketing basic regression models as far more sophisticated than they are.
